one_liner: Hand-written RISC-V Vector 1.0 memcpy, memset and strlen kernels; memcpy averages 2x a board's scalar libc in cache.
what_it_does: A benchmark suite of RVV 1.0 assembly kernels (bench/*.S) with a C harness that times them against the hosted libc, musl's C code, a byte loop and a compiler-vectorized loop, reporting bytes per cycle from 1 byte to 32 MB. Each kernel uses the standard C signature and calling convention (memcpy(dest, src, n), memset(dest, c, n), strlen(s)) but is emitted under macro-generated names such as memcpy_rvv_m4 for LMUL 1, 2, 4 and 8. It is a study and copy source, not a packaged or dispatched libc.
how_it_is_fast: The kernels are RVV strip-mining loops: vsetvli sets vl = min(remaining, VLMAX), so each vle8.v/vse8.v moves a whole register group (128 bytes at LMUL 4 on VLEN 256) and the last partial chunk needs no scalar tail loop. strlen loads with fault-only-first vle8ff.v (or with page-bounded plain loads in the page_aligned variant) and finds the NUL with vmseq.vi plus vfirst.m. The baseline appears to be scalar code: on the X60 the board's libc memset is no faster than musl's 64-bit SWAR C at 16 KB and 1.46x slower at 265 KB (derived from page data).
when_to_use: Writing or picking memcpy, memset or strlen for an RVV 1.0 core whose libc has no vector path. On a SpacemiT X60 (VLEN 256) the 7-instruction LMUL-4 memcpy ran 2.7x libc at 1-16 KB and was never slower over 233 sizes.
Freestanding, embedded or custom-libc RISC-V builds: the harness builds freestanding (nolibc.h) for rv64gcv and rv32 Zve32f, and the kernels need nothing but the vector unit.

Tuning LMUL and alignment strategy for a specific core: rvv-bench-results publishes the same kernels measured on many cores (SpacemiT X60, SiFive P870, XuanTie C920V2, Tenstorrent X280, CanMV K230 and others) next to instruction-throughput tables.
In-cache fills and copies (up to about 1 MB), where LMUL-4 memset ran 1.6-1.8x libc and memcpy 2.0-2.7x on the X60.
Long strings on the X60: the LMUL-1 vle8ff strlen held about 2x libc from 1 MB to 16 MB.
when_not_to_use: Buffers larger than the caches: memcpy and memset converge to 1.0-1.1x libc from 8 MB up on the X60 because DRAM bandwidth is the limit.

strlen without per-core tuning: the LMUL-4 variant is slower than libc at 135 of 262 sizes and runs at 0.65-0.7x above about 280 KB, and the best in-cache variant (page_aligned_m8, 4.9x at 16 KB) drops to 0.64x at 260 KB.

Systems whose libc already dispatches an RVV routine: the measured gap is against an unnamed, apparently scalar board libc. A glibc RVV memcpy IFUNC series was still unmerged in patchwork per search snippets.
XTheadVector 0.7.1 cores (C906/C910) or RISC-V cores without V: the kernels are RVV 1.0 only.
Overlapping buffers or a drop-in libc: there is no memmove kernel, no ifunc or hwprobe dispatch and no packaging, so you must extract, rename and wire the routines in yourself.

integration.dependencies: none for the kernels; the harness uses the repo's nolibc.h and optionally Linux perf_event for user-mode cycle counting
integration.min_toolchain: GCC or Clang with an RVV 1.0 assembler (-march=rv64gcv). CI builds with clang-20 and Ubuntu's riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc; the X60 results label the compiler clang 18.
integration.platforms: RISC-V with the V 1.0 extension (rv64gcv; rv32 with Zve32f also builds in CI); not XTheadVector
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the kernels are stateless leaf routines that touch only argument, temporary and vector registers
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the C signatures and calling convention match memcpy, memset and strlen, but the symbols are macro-generated (memcpy_rvv_m4 and so on through bench/template.S), so you extract and rename them; there is no memmove semantics and no runtime dispatch

gotchas: The memcpy page's 'scalar_autovec' row tracks libc within about 1% at most sizes (geomean 1.02x), which fits the compiler turning the byte loop into a libc memcpy call, so that row is not real auto-vectorized code. Memset's scalar_autovec row, by contrast, reaches 1.56x libc at 16 KB and 1.80x at 265 KB, so a plain C loop built with -march=rv64gcv already captures much of the memset gain (derived from page data).

Each plotted point is a trimmed mean of the middle 60% of 10-64 single-call timings (bench.h), not a median. Misalignment is re-randomized per repetition, and before every timed call the destination is pre-written by a libc memset outside the timed region, so copies hit a warm destination. Small sizes include call and cycle-counter overhead (the same for every implementation).
LMUL choice changes the verdict per kernel: LMUL-1 memset loses to libc at 137 of 245 sizes (0.70x at 16 KB) while LMUL 4 wins, and LMUL-8 memcpy dips to 0.78x at its worst size.

strlen_rvv_page_aligned hardcodes 4096-byte pages and, after the first page boundary, issues plain VLMAX-byte loads. That is safe only while VLEN*LMUL/8 <= 4096 bytes (VLEN up to 4096 bits at LMUL 8); CI validates the kernels in QEMU at VLEN 128-1024 with tail-agnostic all-ones on and off.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only RISC-V Vector entry here: sve-string-routines-benchmarks and Arm Optimized Routines target Arm SVE/NEON, and tinymembench and copies-and-fills target older ARM boards. Pick rvv-bench for RVV 1.0 cores and for per-core LMUL tuning data; pick Arm Optimized Routines when you need a maintained, packaged library on Arm.
verified_claims_summary: On a SpacemiT X60 (K1, 1.6 GHz, VLEN 256), the author's cycle-counter harness (-march=rv64gcv -O3, compiler labelled clang 18) measured the plain LMUL-4 RVV memcpy at 2.0x the board's unnamed libc by geomean over 233 sizes (4.7x at 66 B, 2.7x at 1-16 KB, 1.07x from 8 MB, never slower) and memset at 1.5x (parity from 8 MB). strlen was mixed: LMUL 4 was 1.15x by geomean and slower at 135 of 262 sizes, while LMUL 1 was about 2x at multi-MB sizes (ratios derived from page data).
status_note: Active (135 commits, last on 2026-08-14; CI validates every bench kernel under QEMU at four VLENs) and MIT-licensed, so copyable: lift the few-instruction kernels you need and rename the MX() symbols rather than linking the repo.
